Cpt_801.c: Walnut wooden book cover with ivory insets, made in the third or fourth century AD in Egypt. Some of the oldest known examples of wooden book covers are preserved in the Chester Beatty. This binding, cut from precious walnut, retains traces of leather as well as ivory insets carved with laurel ornament. The central panel (now missing) was also carved ivory and the visible damage to the walnut was probably a result of its forcible removal. Although the loss of this panel makes it impossible to know more about the book it once covered, such precious materials are a tell-tale sign of its luxury status. Book covers adorned with ivory, gold, silver and jewels are known as treasure bindings. While the oldest complete examples date to the fifth or sixth century, this ivory-inlaid cover, dated to the third or fourth century, may represent the earliest surviving treasure binding.

Cpt_802.c: Wooden board of cedar for a bookbinding with traces of leather and fragments of carved ivory insets, made in Egypt in the third or fourth century AD. Hollows in the shape of rosettes, now missing their insets, were probably the location of leather fasteners.

Cpt_810_1.c: One of a pair wooden boards with recess and carved decoration made in the 2nd or 3rd century AD in Egypt. These boards are among the early bindings published by Berthe van Regemorter (1879–1964) in 1958. The unusual interior hollows have led some to question whether these were in fact binding boards. Holes through the front and aligned along the edges, may have been used to attach the now lost textblock to the boards. Holes in the lower board retain fragments of leather thongs, while small pieces of metal in the holes along the spine edge were perhaps used to attach the covers to one another. The lower cover was repaired, probably at the time of its discovery in the early twentieth century, using sand and glue. The decorative crosses suggest a Christian purpose.

W_022.c: Parchment codex containing the Old Testament books Genesis to Ruth written in Latin in black ink around 1153 for Walsingham Priory, Norfolk (England), around the time the monastery was founded. It is the first (and only extant) volume of a complete Bible. Initial letters are written in red, green or blue ink, some with additional pen flourishes. Important texts, rubrics and introductory words are written in alternating green and red. Marginal notes and corrections were added by a contemporary hand in brown ink. Some rubricator notes are still visible in the margins. Each book (or prefatory text) is illustrated with an historiated or decorated initial (10 in total). The manuscript was purchased by Edith Beatty in 1921 from Fitzroy Fenwick (Phillipps Collection 4769) as a gift for Chester Beatty. W_080.c: Parchment codex containing Garden of Knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia, primarily an edited version of Thomas de Cantimpré's On the nature of things (Liber de naturis rerum) with variations and interpolations (including quotations from Gervase of Tilbury), written, edited and illuminated by jurist Jean Reynaud between 1386-1425 probably in Avignon (France). Thomas de Cantimpré (1201-c. 1272) is best known for his encyclopaedia, compiled between 1230-1245, which purported to contain all the natural history knowledge of his time. It included information on anthropology, zoology, botany, mineralogy, astronomy, astrology and meteorology. Jean Reynaud's version took as his model a rare twenty-two book version of Cantimpré's encyclopaedia. The manuscript was purchased in 1924 from the Phillipps Collection.

W_089.c: A Book of Hours written on parchment and illuminated between 1485-1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. The illuminations are attributed to at least five different hands: the Master of the Echevinage de Rouen (8), Jean Bourdichon (2), a follower of Jean Fouquet (6), the Master of Jean Charpentier (9), and the workshop of the Master of the Echevinage (calendar miniatures and secondary illumination). The pink velvet cover dates to a rebinding, probably in the 17th century. The link with Rouen is confirmed in the suffrages and litany, but not the calendar of feasts. Almost all folios with full-page miniatures were removed from the bound volume in the 20th century. The three miniatures that remain in the book are the Annuncation (f.35r), Harrowing of Hell (f.74r) and Ego sum (f.116v).

W_089_f_13.t: Four Symbols of the Evangelists from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_13.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. The four symbols of the evangelists are depicted on a blue ground, each holding a scroll identifying their associated saint: the winged man (S. Matheus), the lion (S. Marcus), the ox (Sanctus Lucas), and the eagle (S. Iohannus). INICIUM SANCTI EVANGELII is written on the golden frame, decorated with acanthus scrolls. The text for the Gospel Lessons, beginning with John, continues on the verso. A two-line decorative initial contains blue flowers.

W_089_f_16.t: Pietà from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_16.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. At the base of a T-shaped cross, a group of women and St John kneel, pray and grief around the body of Jesus which rests on the mantle of his mother Mary. John holds his head. A jar of anointing oils in the lower right is presumably included to identify one of the women as Mary Magdalene. A castle is depicted in the background. OBSECRO TE DOMINA is written on the golden frame, introducing a section of prayers to the Virgin. The rubic, 'cy ensuivent plusieurs honnes et devotes oroisons a nostre dame' is written on the recto below the concluding text to the Gospel Lessons (Mark) which finishes with a decorative line filler.

W_089_f_24.t: Tree of Jesse from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_24.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to Jean Bourdichon. Jesse sits on a throne with a branching tree rising from behind him. This is a visual representation of the genealogy of Jesus, who depicted as an infant with his mother Mary above. The other ancestors are not identified but generally include Solomon and King David. LIBER GENERACIONIS IHESUS CHIRISTI is written on the gold frame. Lined only on the recto.

W_089_f_30.t: Christ taking leave of his mother from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_30.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The painting depicts Mary kneeling in prayer before a seated Jesus who holds an open book. A group of men are depicted in conversation in the background. The painting introduces the five prayers of St John the Evangelist to the Virgin, announced as Five Sorrows of the Virgin. The rubric on the recto reads, 'Cy ensuivent les cinq douleurs nostre dame contenants cinq resquestes'.

W_089_f_40.t: Visitation from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_40.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Mary stands in a landscape with her cousin Elizabeth who is pregnant with John the Baptist. She kneels as she recognises the significance of Mary's own pregnancy. A city with castle on a hill is depicted across a waterway in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIU[M] MEU[M] is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Lauds of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorated initials introduce different sections of the text, one is decorated with a bird, the other with strawberries.

W_089_f_45.t: Nativity from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_45.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. In a stable-like interior with stone walls and wooden roof, a haloed Mary knees before the infant Jesus, Joseph knees behind her. An ox and ass sit behind the infant. Several shepherds, including one playing the bagpipes, watch through windows and the doorway in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM MEUM is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Prime of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of the text, one illustrated with a butterfly, the other with a bird.

W_089_f_47.t: Annunciation to the Shepherds from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_47.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. A night scene, illuminated by heavenly light from above and a camp figure below. A group of shepherds and shepherdesses in a landscape, some holding staffs and one playing the bagpipes, are visited by an angel announcing the birth of Jesus. A city is depicted across a waterway in the background. DUES IN ADIUTORIUM ME[EM] is written on the golden architectural frame, introducing Terce of the Virgin. The text on the recto concludes Prime of the Virgin. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one depicts a bird, the other a snail.

W_089_f_49.t: Adoration of the Magi from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_49.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Beneath a wooden-framed space, Mary sits with the infant in her lap, Joseph stands behind them. On the left side of the composition, three kings (one who has removed his crown) present gifts to the baby. A star is depicted in the upper left corner, with a riverscape in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM MEUM is written on the golden architectural frame, the opening words to Sext of the Virgin. The text on the recto concludes Terce of the Virgin and includes the rubric 'Ad Sextam.'

W_089_f_51.t: The Circumcision from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_51.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Within an interior setting, a group of people crowd around a decorative table (altar). Mary and Joseph stand on the left while a male and female figure hold the infant Jesus as he is circumcised. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM is written on the elaborate golden architectural frame. The text of None of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one with flowers the other with a bird.

W_089_f_53.t: Dormition of the Virgin from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_53.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. The apostles stand and kneel around the deathbed of the Virgin Mary. Some hold their hands in prayer while others read from open books, including presumably Peter who also appears to be holding an aspergillum (instrument for sprinkling holy water). Another apostle holds a palm leaf, possibly John. The Resurrected Jesus stands with a staff, both his side and hand wounds visible, and offers a sign of blessing with his left hand. DEUS IN ADIUTORIU[M] is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Vespers of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of the text, one encloses a small bird.

W_089_f_54.t: Coronation of the Virgin from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_54.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. The Virgin Mary kneels as the Resurrected Jesus, wearing a purple cloak, places a crown on her head, signifying her role as Queen of Heaven. She kneels before God who is depicted as an old man wearing the papal tiara and seated in a covered throne. He holds the orb and cross (globus cruciger). The Holy Spirit in the form of a dove is depicted between God and Jesus. A choir of angels fill the background. CONVERTE NOS DEUS is written on the golden architectural frame, the opening words of Compline of the Virgin. The text on the recto includes the concluding prayers for Vespers of the Virgin and the rubric 'Ad completorium'. One two-line decorative initial contains flowers.

W_089_f_57.t: Man of Sorrow from a book of hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_57.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The resurrected Christ stands in his open tomb flanked by the Virgin Mary and St John. The composition may have been inspired by a print of the same subject by Martin Schongauer (1435/50–1491). Written on the bejewelled and gilded trompe-l'oeil frame, D[OMI]NE LABIA MEA APERIES, the opening words of Matins of the Holy Cross. The text continues on the verso. Three two-line decorated initials introduce new sections of text, one enclosing a small bird, the other two contain flowers.

W_089_f_59.t: Pentecost from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_59.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The Virgin Mary with a group of apostles and other women stand in a church-like setting as flaming tongues descend from the upper left. St James the Greater is identified by his pilgrim staff and scallop-emblazoned hat. D[OMI]NE LABIA MEA APERIES is written on the frame, which is decorated with a marble effect. The text for Matins of the Holy Spirit continues on the verso. Three two-line decorated initials open different sections of the text, each contain a small bird.

W_089_f_61.t: Deposition from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_61.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. STABAT MATER DOLOROSA is written on the golden architectural frame. Two men stand on ladders lowering the body of Jesus from the T-shaped cross, aided by a third man (perhaps Joseph of Arimathea) standing in front of the cross. Mary kneels in prayer, John holds the feet of Jesus and a woman (possibly Mary Magdalene) holds his hand. Three other figures are depicted in the background. The text, a hymn to Our Lady of sorrows, continues on the verso, each verse opens with a small decorative initial and each line is finished with decorative line-fillers.

W_089_f_65.t: Bathsheba bathing from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_65.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to Jean Bourdichon. Bathsheba is seen bathing in a fountain, with King David watching from the window of his castle in the background. DOMINE IN FURORE is written on the gold frame. The text on the verso is from the Penitential Psalms.

W_089_f_89.t: Three persons of the Trinity from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_89.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The three figures of God the Father, Jesus and the Holy Spirit are seated in a triple niche with scalloped domes. The each hold an orb and cross (globus cruciger) in one hand and offers a blessing with the other. The central figure is winged. The whole setting appears to be floating. The golden frame is given a marble finish. The text on the verso begins 'Memoire de la benoiste trinite'. A second prayer 'Omnipotens sempiterne deus qui dedisti', opens with the Trinity within the historiated initial O. The text for 'De saint michiel archange' includes St Michael within an historiated initial D.

W_089_f_90.t: St Michael and the Devil from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_90.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. In a landscape, the armoured Archangel Michael fights two demons. One, trapped beneath his feet, attempts to bite the archangel's leg through his armour, the other clings to Michael's shield. No text is written on the golden framed, which is decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves, and therefore the opening words 'MICHAEL ARCHANGELE VENI' are missing from the following prayer. The text on the verso includes prayers to the Archangel Michael and the rubric, 'De monseigneur st michiel larchangel.'

W_089_f_91.t: Archangel Gabriel from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_91.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. The Archangel Gabriel, with bejewelled and billowing mantle, holds a cross and scroll which reads, 'Ave gratia plena.' He stands in a large gothic stone cathedral with groin vault. The golden tiles are decorated with blue letters. No text is written on the golden frame, and therefore the first words for the suffrage to the Archangel Gabriel are missing. The text on the recto includes the conclusion of prayers to St Michael and the rubric 'De saint gabriel larchange'. A two-line decorated initial depicts St Micheal.

W_089_f_93.t: St John the Baptist in the wilderness from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_93.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. John the Baptist wearing his camel-hair tunic sits on a rock in a landscape with a sheep. He has a golden halo and holds a cross. PUER QUI NATUS E(ST) NOBIS is written on the bejewelled and gilded frame. The prayer on the verso opens 'Deus qui presentem diem hoborabilem.' St John the Baptist is depicted within the historiated initial D and St Peter is depicted in the historiated initial D, opening a prayer to 'De saint pierre'.

W_089_f_96.t: St George and the Dragon from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen
W_089_f_96.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St George, clothed in golden armour, sits on a white horse from which he slays the dragon. The bones of children the dragon has already eaten in the lower right corner. The princess, whose life is thus saved, stands on the left behind George, while the king and queen (her parents) watch from the top of their castle in the background. SALVE MARTIR GLORIOSE is written in the golden frame, decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves. The text on the recto includes prayers to St Laurence and St Denis and the rubric, 'Memoire de saint george'. Two two-line decorative initials contain the gridiron of St Laurence and the beheaded head of St Denis.

W_089_f_100.t: Martyrdom of St Sebastian from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_100.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St Sebastian, tied against a tree, is shot by two archers, multiple arrows already protrude from his body. A figure ties ropes around his feet. Three figures on the left direct the action against Sebastian. A stone, walled city is depicted in the background. O QUAM MIRA REFULSIT GRACIA is written on the golden frame, decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves. The suffrage to St Sebastian continues on the verso. A two-line decorative initial contains an arrow, the saint's attribute.

W_089_f_101.t: St Martin and the Beggar from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_101.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St Martin, sitting on a white horse before the gates to a city, uses his sword to cut his cloak. This is presents to 'the beggar', a man with crutch and wooden leg. Three angels and God hold scrolls written with prayers to the saint. O MARTINE O PIE QUAM PIUM is written on the golden frame. The text on the recto includes prayers to St Nicolas and St Germain and the rubric, 'Memoire de monseigneur saint martin'. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one contains St Nicholas.

W_094.c: A book of hours for the use of Paris in Latin and French, produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. It is written in a gothic script called ‘textualis quadrata’ using dark brown and red ink on parchment and bound in an 18th-century brown leather cover. There are 19 miniatures with realistically-rendered floral borders; 6 remain in the bound volume (ff. 1r, 3r, 11r, 12v, 17r, 23r). Eighteen folios, 14 miniatures (ff.4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 15, 19, 21, 25, 50, 69,126, 211, 242) and 4 text folios (ff.63, 68, 91, 98), were removed from the manuscript around 1954. The book was rebound in the eighteenth century, and pages were repaired and almost certainly removed at that time, likely in response to historic water damage (which is evident throughout the manuscript). A note in French on the fly leaf (f. iiiv), probably written around the time of the rebinding, records the prior removal of several folios with miniatures. W_094_f_04.t: March (recto), Hunting in April (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_04.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for March 15-31, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a particular saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St Benedict of Nursia (21 March) and the Feast of the Annunciation (25 March). On the verso is a hunting scene, introducing the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month,' here associated with April. The ivy-leaf borders are inhabited (in the upper margin) by two putti (wingless cherubs) fighting with shields. In the lower margin, a coat of arms is held between two eagles.

On the recto is a scene of a picnic, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', here associated with May. The borders are filled with realistically-rendered blue violets inhabited (in the upper margin) by a bird. In the lower margin, a coat of arms supported from a pole which rests on the shoulders of two putti (wingless cherubs), each standing on a short, four-legged stool. On the verso is the calendar for May 1-15, divided into four columns. W_094_f_07.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. W_094_f_19.t: St Matthew introducing the Gospel lesson of Luke, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_19.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a portrait of Matthew seated on a canopied throne writing his gospel. His symbol, a winged man, holds the book. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted blue and white columbines (Aquilegia) inhabited by butterflies. A putto with a spear and heron are in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held by two putti below. The portraits of Matthew and Luke incorrectly placed. Here the painting introduces the text for Luke and his name (lucam) appears in red below. Three lines of text read 'In illo tempore, missus est angelus Gabriel a Deo in...' (At that time, the Angel Gabriel was sent of God into...). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_21.t: St Luke introducing the Gospel Lesson of Matthew, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_21.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a portrait of Luke seated before a desk sharpening his pen, a scroll falls over the desk before him. His symbol, a winged ox, rests its hoof on a book. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted blue periwinkles (Vinca) inhabited by birds and butterflies. A putto and bear wrestle in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held between two snails below. The portraits of Matthew and Luke incorrectly placed. Here the painting introduces the text for Matthew and his name (matheum) appears in red below. Three lines of text read 'Cum natus esset Iesus in Bethlehem Iuda...' (When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah...). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_25.t: The Annunciation introducing Matins of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_25.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Annunciation. While Mary reads, the archangel Gabriel appears and announces her pregnancy. A vase of lilies rest on the floor between then. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted white lilies (Lilium), also known as the Madonna Lily. The tall stems of the flowers twist to create eight roundels in which prophets and ancestors of Mary are painted. The painting introduces Matins of the Virgin. The three lines of text begin, 'Domine labia mea aperies' (Lord, you will open my lips). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_50.t: The Visitation introducing Lauds of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_50.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Visitation. Elizabeth, pregnant with John the Baptist, embraces her also pregnant cousin Mary. They stand in a landscape, while Joseph walks out of the frame to the left. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted strawberries (Fragaria) inhabited by butterflies. A putto plays with a dog, while a cat hisses in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held between a dog and cat below. The painting introduces Lauds of the Virgin. The three lines of text begin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende' (God, help me). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised strawberries.

W_094_f_63.t: Prime of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_63.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Hour of Prime of the Virgin, usually read around sunrise. On the verso is an historiated initial V with a half-length portrait of a man wearing an ermine-trimmed cloak. This is probably meant to represent King David, to whom the psalms are traditionally ascribed. The text which follows is from psalm 5, and begins Verba mea auribus percipe (Hear my words). The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains. The mound on the verso is home to a life-like rat.

W_094_f_68.t: Terce of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_68.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Hour of Prime of the Virgin, usually read around sunrise. On the recto is an historiated initial P with a half-length portrait of a nude woman. She is probably meant to represent Eve. The text which follows reads Paradisi porta per evam, and continues on the verso, cunctis clausa est. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders created with chains.

W_094_f_69.t: The Adoration of the Magi introducing Sext of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_69.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the concluding text for the hour of Terce of the Virgin. The rubic for Sext of the Virgin (Ad vi) is written in red at the bottom. The text is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised strawberries. On the verso is a scene of the Adoration of the Magi. May holds the baby Jesus while a procession of figures on horses come to great them with gifts. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted boxwood leaves (Boxus) inhabited by butterflies. A dog faces a porcupine in the upper margin while two bears hold the coat of arms in the lower margin. The painting introduces Sext of the Virgin, usually read around noon. The three lines of text begin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende' (God, help me).

W_094_f_91.t: The Penitential Psalms, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_91.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Penitential Psalms. The recto includes text from psalm 50 which concludes on the verso. The is followed by the Latin word psalmus is written in red and the beginning of psalm 101; Domine exaudi orationem meum (Lord, hear my prayer). Both sides of the folio are decorated with conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised flowers.

W_094_f_98.t: The Litany, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_98.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Litany, which includes invocations for the intercession of various saints. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. W_094_f_126.t: The Office of the Dead, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_126.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Office of the Dead. On the recto an historiated initial A contains a grotesque bird with leaves emanating from its beak. The text is from psalm 119 and begins Ad dominum cum tribularer clamavi (When I was in tribulation I cried to our Lord). The text continues on the verso. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves and suns in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains.

W_094_f_211.t: The Raising of the Cross introducing Sext of the Passion, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_211.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Raising of the Cross or Crucifixion. Jesus is nailed to the cross positioned diagonally across the picture as it is raised upright. The scene is crowded with soldiers and other onlookers. His mother Mary and friends grieve in the lower right. A ship sails on rough waters in the background. The painting is surrounded by blue larkspurs inhabited above by a putto facing a rearing long-horned goat. In the lower margin, the coat of arms is flanked by two donkeys. The scene introduces Sext of the Passion (to be read at noon), and continues on the back. The text on the verso is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders with stylised flowers and acanthus leaves.

W_094_f_242.t: The Baptism of Jesus introducing a prayer to John the Baptist, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_242.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Baptism of Jesus by his cousin John the Baptist. Jesus stands in the Jordan River looking over his shoulder toward God who holds open a book. An angel looks down from mountains above. The painting is surrounded by pink roses inhabited by putti. In the lower margin, the coat of arms is flanked by two wildmen. The scene introduces a prayer to John the Baptist and continues on the back. The text on the verso is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders with stylised flowers.

W_099.c: A rosarium codex written in Latin on parchment with miniatures painted by Simon Bening (1483-1561) made between 1540-1545 in Bruges. The codex is bound in a sixteenth-century Spanish gold-tooled leather binding with two metal clasps. A number of its miniatures were removed from the binding and are now housed separately. A rosarium is a collection of devotions dedicated to the Virgin Mary. One of the most conspicuous features of this richly illuminated example is its purple margins, a distinctive mark of royal ownership. Indeed, this illuminated rosarium was commissioned by either the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (1500–1558) or his son, Philip II, King of Spain (1527–1598). The paintings are the work of Simon Bening, the last of the great masters of Flemish manuscript painting. Bening drew inspiration from his peers, quoting freely from Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer, and he in turn influenced the next generation of artists. W_103_1.t: Calendar from the Chester Beatty Hours
W_103_1.c: Eleven parchment folios from the calendar of the Chester Beatty Book of Hours (February to December), created by the workshop of the Mazarine Master and completed in 1408 in Paris. The manuscript is one of the few securely dated Book of Hours (see colophon, W 103 f.158). All folios have fully illuminated foliate borders (water damage to all borders, especially September to December). Previous foliation (ff.169-178, with 2 folios numbered 171) from a historic rebinding. Miniatures had been removed from the manuscript and sold or otherwise dispersed in 1932, 1939 and 1969. The manuscript was further dis-bound following the Sotheby's sale on 24 June 1969 (lot 58).

W_122.t: Dictys Cretensis' Trojan War (De bello troiano)
W_122.c: Illuminated parchment manuscript containing the fictitious eyewitness account of the Trojan War purportedly by Dictys Cretensis, written and illuminated by Bartholomew Sanvito in the mid to late 15th century in Italy. Each of the six books are introduced with decorative borders and the text includes a total of fifty-five miniatures painted primarily in blue or lilac camaïeu - a type of monochrome using a colour other than grey. The manuscript was made for Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga (1461-1483), whose arms appear on f. 3r. It was purchased by Edith Beatty in November 1925 from the Phillipps Collection and presented as a birthday gift for Chester Beatty in February 1926.

W_129.c: Small parchment scroll (rotuli) containing an archival copy made for the Pachomian Monastic Library, probably at Phbow (Egypt), of Pachomius' Letters 1-3, 7, 10 and 11a, written in Greek (translated from the Coptic original) in the fourth century. Pachomius (d. 346) is credited as the father of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism. He established the first monastery in Upper Egypt and the community quickly grew to 12 large monasteries housing thousands of monks. By the end of the fourth century sister communities had been established in Cappadocia, Syria, Palestine, Italy and Gaul. A collection of his writings and letters was probably assembled by his successors Theodore and Horsiesios. Many of the letters make a mysterious use of the alphabet, which may relate to the ancient Egyptian love of cryptograms, but efforts to decipher them have so far been unsuccessful. W_132.c: Parchment manuscript containing a twelfth-century copy in Greek of a series of homilies by John Chrysostom, John of Damascus, Anastasius Monachus, Hippolytus and others. Each homily is introduced with a decorative heading and an enlarged initial letter in red and blue. The title in the upper margin and rubrics also in red, passages identified by numbers in the margin (45–66). The first two folios and folios 11-15 are later insertions in a later hand. Green leather binding decorated with a gold tooled cross. The manuscript was purchased in October 1924 by John Hope Johnstone, on behalf of A. Chester Beatty, from the Russian Monastery of St Panteleimon (Rossikon) on Mt Athos.

W_133.t: Homilies of St John Chrysostom on the Gospel of John
W_133.c: Parchment manuscript containing a twelfth-century copy in Greek of a series of forty-six homilies (missing number 3) by John Chrysostom on the Gospel of John. An illuminated blue headpiece introduces the first homily, with each successive homily introduced with its number in the upper margin (*ΟΜΙΛΙΑ Δ* = Homily 4) and the passage from John under discussion followed by an enlarged initial letter, all in red. Red leather binding cover decorated with tooled gold cross. The manuscript was purchased in October 1924 by John Hope Johnstone, on behalf of A. Chester Beatty, from the Russian Monastery of St Panteleimon (Rossikon) on Mt Athos.

W_139.c: Manuscript containing a Byzantine Gospel book written in Greek on parchment in the late 11th or early 12th century in modern Turkey or Greece. This deluxe gospel book was produced at the pinnacle of the Byzantine period and demonstrates a high degree of artistic and scribal mastery. Unusually, it retains a late-medieval binding with purple cloth covers, an indicator of its luxury status. Portraits of the evangelists and decorative headings are the focus of illustration and ornament in Byzantine gospel manuscripts. Here, St. Mark pauses from his writing to dip his pen in ink, with additional writing instruments and scrolls laid out on the desk and lectern before him. The gold background, symbolically placing him in a heavenly sphere, suggests divine inspiration. W_147.c: Nikolje Gospels written on parchment in Old Church Slavonic in a Bosnian Cyrillic script with influence from the Raska School, made in Bosnia in the late 14th or early 15th century and probably a product of Royal Scriptorium of Tvrtko I (r. 1377–1391). Each of the four gospels is introduced by a miniature of the Evangelical symbol rather than a portrait of the author: winged man for Matthew (f.ii v), lion for Mark (f.46v), ox for Luke (f.79v) and eagle for John (f.136v). A headpiece (zastavki) with geometrical and vegetal ornament decorates the first page of text of each gospel, with a tail piece at the end of both Matthew and Luke. The headpieces for the gospels of Matthew and Mark include the Bosnian crown. Decorated initials are found on ff. 4v, 5r, 117r, 126r, 135r, 151v, 155r and 164v.

W_158.c: Parchment codex with leather cover containing a Lectionary in Serbian Church Slavonic, dated to the 13th century and attributed to the Raška school. The book contains prayers and the readings for eight Sundays after Pentecost, then for weekdays, martyrs, hierarchs, saints and the dead, Christmas, Epiphany and Sexagesima; it is incomplete.

W_159.c: A single illuminated paper folio preserving the opening of the Gospel of St Matthew in Church Slavonic, probably from a Gospel book, possibly made in the 15th century in Valahia or Walachia in modern Romania. A large headpiece (zastavka) is decorated with interlace branchwork (pletenka) and various decorative features including a bird, human hands, a serpent, cow's head, sun and moon. The decorated initial K, also created using interlace design, terminates in a manicule with two fingers pointing to the text. To the descenders of characters in the bottom line blossom into decorative ornaments.

W_192.t: Wooton's Elements of architecture & Vitruvius' De architectura
W_192.c: Bound manuscript containing Henry Wooton's The Elements of Architecture (1624) followed by an incomplete English translation of Vitruvius' De architectura (30-15 BC), written and illustrated with architectural drawings by Michael Wills (active c. 1721-1777) in Ireland c. 1770. The texts are prefaced by a dedicatory letter by John de Laet to Queen Christiana of Sweden, dated Leyden, 15 May 1649. The gilt-featherwork binding is attributed to Edward Beatty (formerly known as Parliamentary Binder B), made in Dublin c. 1755.

Wx_118.c: Bronze medal commemorating the 1686 Siamese embassy to France designed by the royal medallist, Jean Mauger (1648–1722) and produced 1686-89 in Paris. A portrait of King Louis XIV (1638–1715) of France in profile is inscribed: LUDOVICUS MAGNUS REX CHRISTIANISS. On the reverse is an image of the French King receiving the Siamese ambassadors at Versailles, inscribed and signed: FAMA VIRTUTIS | ORATORES REGIS SIAM (Virtuous Fame, Ambassadors of the King of Siam), M. DC. LXXXVI. | MAUGER. F (1686 made by Mauger). The three Siamese ambassadors, Kosa Pan, Ok-luang Kanlaya Ratchamaitri, and Ok-khun Sisawan Wacha, kneel before Louis XIV and present a gift.
